cards.title: Google Ads Diagnostic Tree: Top-Down Root Cause Analysis
cards.summary: A top-down order of investigation for diagnosing Google Ads performance declines, from business level down to the submetric.
cards.use_when: Paid search or Shopping performance has dipped and you must decide whether to act, what to change, and in what order before touching the account.
steps: Never start at the metric the client or dashboard flagged. Start at the business level and ask what materially changed: revenue, margin, offer, site. If business-level numbers are up, a 10% ROAS dip in your fifth-largest spender may not warrant investigation at all.

Move down one level at a time: channel level (did Meta, email or organic change, since a brand search campaign is largely dependent on Meta spend?), then campaign type, then specific campaign, then finally the submetric.
At each level ask 'why' before descending. Diagnose the metric (CPA up? volume down?) to route to the relevant submetric branch.

Only act once you can complete the sentence: 'This campaign is underperforming because [metric] dropped, driven by [submetric], caused by [trigger], which is the root cause.' If you cannot finish that sentence, do not touch the account.
This ordering is the source's asserted separator between strong and weak media buyers; treat it as a working heuristic rather than a proven performance benchmark.
caveats: Source is explicit that most 'broken' accounts are simply misread, so a cross-channel sanity check belongs before any in-platform change.
Requires access to business-level revenue and margin data, not just ad platform numbers.

cards.title: Diagnosing Rising CPC: Three Causes and When It Actually Matters
cards.summary: CPC is treated as a vanity metric; diagnose quality score, new auction entrants, and premium auction entry before reacting.
cards.use_when: Cost per click has risen in Google Ads, Meta or TikTok and you need to decide whether it signals a real problem for store acquisition cost.
steps: Check CPA first, not CPC. The source's position is that CPCs are a vanity metric on Google, Meta and TikTok because they only matter at the extremes. Higher CPC with proportionally higher conversion rate keeps CPA flat and is acceptable; higher CPC with flat conversion rate is the problem case.

If CPC is the issue, test three explanations: (1) Quality score components deteriorated, with ad relevance and expected CTR being more actionable than landing page experience; (2) a new competitor entered the auction, verified by comparing Auction Insights before and after the dip point; (3) you moved to more premium auctions after changing tROAS or another bidding strategy.
For the premium-auction case, ask whether the higher-cost clicks are actually higher quality. If conversion rate has not risen to offset the CPC increase, the premium auctions are not paying off.
Adjust bidding strategy, creative or market coverage based on which cause you confirm rather than cutting spend reflexively.
caveats: Landing page experience is the hardest quality-score component to move: it depends on dev work and Google's re-crawl/re-score cycle, and the source reports cases taking weeks to months to turn around even after the site was fixed.
Google's quality score internals and re-crawl cadence are opaque and change; verify the current interface and behaviour before relying on any specific component.

cards.title: Diagnosing Falling Conversion Rate: Tracking, Landing Page, Audience, Learning, Offer
cards.summary: A five-step check for conversion-rate declines, ordered from tracking errors to offer changes, that applies to platform and storefront conversion alike.
cards.use_when: Ad platform conversion rate or site conversion rate has dropped and you need to separate measurement artefacts from real storefront problems before rebuilding anything.
steps: Check tracking first: has the pixel or tag stopped firing, or are you reading a window shorter than the actual conversion lag? Conversion-by-time views exist for exactly this; a bad tracking setup makes conversion rate look broken when nothing on the platform changed.

Check whether the landing page materially changed: a different URL, a price change, a redirect, added upsells or cross-sells, or altered merchandising. The source calls this probably the number one real cause of conversion-rate declines.

Check whether the audience changed: read search term reports for new, non-converting terms, and review whether the bidding strategy change pushed you toward a different audience. Low congruency between query, ad and landing page depresses conversion.
Check whether the learning phase reset. Large structural account changes push Google Ads back into learning, during which it enters wrong auctions and drives poor traffic.
Check whether the offer changed: expired promo, removed discount, or an altered free-shipping threshold all depress conversion rate independently of ads.
caveats: Conversion lag means short-window reads systematically understate conversion rate; always compare like-for-like windows.
The source gives no numeric thresholds, so treat the ordering as a diagnostic sequence, not a ranked statistical model.

cards.title: Diagnosing Volume Declines: Impressions, Impression Share and CTR
cards.summary: When efficiency holds but volume falls, trace it to clicks, then to impressions lost to budget versus bid, then to CTR.
cards.use_when: Google Ads revenue or spend has fallen while CPA is stable, and you need to decide whether to raise budget, raise bids, or change creative.
steps: Identify the branch: if efficiency (CPA/ROAS) is unchanged but volume is down, the problem is clicks. Clicks decompose into impressions and CTR.

For impressions, distinguish impression share lost to budget from impression share lost to rank using the platform's impression share columns. If you are hitting your daily budget cap, you are losing share to budget and simply need more spend.

If impressions AND click volume are both down, the source says it is almost certainly not budget — you are being throttled by bid, which is a product of quality score, new competitors and auction aggressiveness. Troubleshoot those three.

For CTR declines, check ad fatigue (source calls this rare on Google, more plausible on search ads than Shopping), audience mismatch via search term reports, seasonal or dated ad copy, and competitor pricing. On Shopping particularly, a competitor running a 20-30% discount on the same product explains a one-for-one CTR drop.
Add the 'search impression share lost to rank' column to your reporting to track the competitive dimension.
caveats: The bid's composition (quality score, competition, aggression) is the source's explanation of platform behaviour; algorithms and available columns change, so verify in the current interface.
Ad fatigue is explicitly described as rare on Google — do not default to refreshing creative as the first response.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Competitor Price Monitoring to Pull Products Before Margin Erosion
cards.summary: A real-time competitor price script that de-prioritises or pulls products from Shopping rather than matching discounts to zero margin.
cards.use_when: Shopping CTR or product-level ROAS drops on specific SKUs and you suspect a competitor has discounted the identical product.
steps: Set up automated monitoring of your biggest competitors' product pages for price changes, so you learn about their discount in real time rather than after a week of poor performance.

Define the rule in advance: when a competitor drops price by roughly 20-30% into no-margin territory, pull the product from the auction or de-prioritise it within the campaign structure rather than discounting to match.

The reasoning is that continuing to force spend at the old price cannot be profitable once ROAS falls off a cliff, while matching the discount erodes gross margin to near nothing. Choosing not to compete on that SKU preserves margin.
Reintroduce the product when the competitor's discount ends.
This is a documented single-client approach — a large sunglasses wholesaler — so treat the outcome as an example of the technique, not a benchmark.
caveats: Pulling products changes campaign structure; the source elsewhere warns that large structural changes trigger learning resets, so weigh the scale of the edit.
Competitor page scraping must be done within legal and terms-of-service constraints and on systems you own or are permitted to monitor.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Fix Before Rebuild: Avoiding the Learning-Phase Death Spiral
cards.summary: Default to targeted fixes over rebuilds because every rebuild triggers a learning reset that can deepen the decline.
cards.use_when: A Google Ads account is underperforming and you are considering restructuring campaigns or the account to fix it.
steps: Treat rebuild as the last resort. The source's default is to apply fixes first, because any rebuild triggers a learning reset that enters wrong auctions and drives poor traffic, making performance worse.
The dangerous pattern is: decline → big change → deeper decline → bigger change, looping until the account is in a terrible position. Break the loop by forcing a fix attempt first.

Estimate the expected impact of each candidate fix honestly. If the gap to baseline is large, a headline tweak will not bridge it; keep refining the fix until you believe it is strong enough to close the gap.
Only rebuild when fixes have failed or cannot plausibly make a material enough difference to return to historical performance.
This is the source's stated opinion about managing Google Ads accounts, not a universal rule across platforms.
caveats: Some accounts genuinely need a restructure; this guidance is about sequencing, not prohibition.
Learning-phase behaviour and reset triggers are platform-specific and change over time; verify current behaviour.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Bundling Versus Isolating Fixes: Choosing Based on Severity
cards.summary: Decide whether to apply one fix at a time for learning, or many at once to rescue a severe decline.
cards.use_when: A storefront or paid media metric has dropped and you are deciding how many changes to ship in the same iteration.
steps: Assess severity first. If the situation is dire, the source accepts throwing the kitchen sink — you do not care which change worked, you just need the problem fixed.

If the decline is mild, isolate variables so you know what actually worked. If you ship nine changes and performance recovers, you learn nothing and cannot solve the problem next time without again throwing the kitchen sink.
Before shipping a bundled set, ask whether the changes could confound each other so much that no conclusion is drawable. If confounded, either isolate or accept you are trading learning for speed.
Allow enough time after the fix to observe whether it worked before layering another fix.
Prioritise fixes by expected impact, and be honest about whether a given change can plausibly move the metric that is actually broken.
caveats: This is a judgement framework, not a statistical experiment design; the source does not specify sample sizes or significance thresholds.
Grouping fixes sacrifices causal attribution — record what you changed so the next diagnosis has a history.

cards.title: Pre-Investigation Checks Before Touching Any Ad Account
cards.summary: Three checks — change history, attribution latency, cross-channel sanity — that should precede any in-platform action.
cards.use_when: A stakeholder reports a performance problem in Google Ads and you are tempted to adjust settings immediately.
steps: Check change history first. Do not change anything you do not yet understand; the change that caused the decline may already be logged there.
Check attribution latency. Conversion-by-time views reveal whether the 'decline' is just conversions that have not yet been attributed in the window you are reading.

Run a cross-channel sanity check. The source's claim is that most accounts that appear broken are not broken at all — you are misreading them or reading the wrong window. Confirm the problem is real and belongs to Google before working on Google.
Only after these three checks do you begin top-down drill-down.
Together these form the source's 'don't touch it until you can explain it' principle.
caveats: Change history does not capture every external factor (competitor moves, seasonality, market shifts), so absence of a logged change does not mean nothing changed.
Requires read access to multiple channel dashboards and to attribution settings.
